entries.df4034d9241356e058e434435062917283bbc47f: <div sID="gen17199" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="3" osisID="Jer.3" sID="Jer.3"/> <div eID="gen17199" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17200" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen17201" type="x-p"/> The foregoing chapter was wholly taken up with reproofs and threatenings against the people of God, for their apostasies from him; but in this chapter gracious invitations and encouragements are given them to return and repent, notwithstanding the multitude and greatness of their provocations, which are here specified, to magnify the mercy of God, and to show that as sin abounded grace did much more abound. Here, I. It is further shown how bad they had been and how well they deserved to be quite abandoned, and yet how ready God was to receive them into his favour upon their repentance, <reference osisRef="Jer.3.1-Jer.3.5">ver. 1-5</reference>. II. The impenitence of Judah, and their persisting in sin, are aggravated from the judgments of God upon Israel, which they should have taken warning by, <reference osisRef="Jer.3.6-Jer.3.11">ver. 6-11</reference>. III. Great encouragements are given to these backsliders to return and repent, and promises made of great mercy which God had in store for them, and which he would prepare them for by bringing them home to himself, <reference osisRef="Jer.3.12-Jer.3.19">ver. 12-19</reference>. IV. The charge renewed against them for their apostasy from God, and the invitation repeated to return and repent, to which are here added the words that are put in their mouth, which they should make use of in their return to God, <reference osisRef="Jer.3.20-Jer.3.25">ver. 20-25</reference>.
entries.d4aa4ac35fc8291838cf88b6d6bd3c82e95c4049: <div eID="gen17201" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen17200" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">The Wickedness of Israel. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 620.)</title> <div sID="gen17202" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> They say, If a man put away his wife, and she go from him, and become another man's, shall he return unto her again? shall not that land be greatly polluted? but thou hast played the harlot with many lovers; yet return again to me, saith the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> . <hi type="super">2</hi> Lift up thine eyes unto the high places, and see where thou hast not been lien with. In the ways hast thou sat for them, as the Arabian in the wilderness; and thou hast polluted the land with thy whoredoms and with thy wickedness. <hi type="super">3</hi> Therefore the showers have been withholden, and there hath been no latter rain; and thou hadst a whore's forehead, thou refusedst to be ashamed. <hi type="super">4</hi> Wilt thou not from this time cry unto me, My father, thou <hi type="italic">art</hi> the guide of my youth? <hi type="super">5</hi> Will he reserve <hi type="italic">his anger</hi> for ever? will he keep <hi type="italic">it</hi> to the end? Behold, thou hast spoken and done evil things as thou couldest. <div eID="gen17202" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17203" type="x-p"/> These verses some make to belong to the sermon in the foregoing chapter, and they open a door of hope to those who receive the conviction of the reproofs we had there; God wounds that he may heal. Now observe here, <div eID="gen17203" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17204" type="x-p"/> I. How basely this people had forsaken God and gone a whoring from him. The charge runs very high here. 1. They had multiplied their idols and their idolatries. To have admitted one strange God among them would have been bad enough, but they were insatiable in their lustings after false worships: <hi type="italic">Thou hast played the harlot with many lovers,</hi> <reference osisRef="Jer.3.1">v. 1</reference>. She had become a common prostitute to idols; not a foolish deity was set up in all the neighbourhood but the Jews would have it quickly. Where was a high place in the country but they had had an idol in it? <reference osisRef="Jer.3.2">v. 2</reference>. Note, In repentance it is good to make sorrowful reflections upon the particular acts of sin we have been guilty of, and the several places and companies where it has been committed, that we may give glory to God and take shame to ourselves by a particular confession of it. 2. They had sought opportunity for their idolatries, and had sent about to enquire for new gods: <hi type="italic">In the</hi> high—<hi type="italic">ways hast thou sat for them,</hi> as Tamar when she put on the disguise of <hi type="italic">a harlot</hi> (<reference osisRef="Gen.38.14">Gen. xxxviii. 14</reference>), and as the <hi type="italic">foolish woman,</hi> that sits to <hi type="italic">call passengers, who go right on their way,</hi> <reference osisRef="Prov.9.14-Prov.9.15">Prov. ix. 14, 15</reference>. <hi type="italic">As the Arabian in the wilderness</hi>—the <hi type="italic">Arabian huckster</hi> (so some), that courts customers, or waits for the merchants to get a good bargain and forestal the market—or the <hi type="italic">Arabian thief</hi> (so others), that watches for his prey; so had they waited either to court new gods to come among them (the newer the better, and the more fond they were of them) or to court others to join with them in their idolatries. They were not only sinners, but Satans, not only traitors themselves, but tempters to others. 3. They had grown very impudent in sin. They not only polluted themselves, but <hi type="italic">their land, with their whoredoms and with their wickedness</hi> (<reference osisRef="Jer.3.2">v. 2</reference>); for it was universal and unpunished, and so became a national sin. And yet (<reference osisRef="Jer.3.3">v. 3</reference>), "<hi type="italic">Thou hadst a whore's forehead,</hi> a brazen face of thy own. <hi type="italic">Thou refusedst to be ashamed;</hi> thou didst enough to shame thee for ever, and yet wouldst not take shame to thyself." Blushing is the colour of virtue, or at least a relic of it; but those that are past shame (we say) are past hope. Those that have an adulterer's heart, if they indulge that, will come at length to have a whore's forehead, void of all shame and modesty. 4. They abounded in all manner of sin. They polluted the land not only with <hi type="italic">their whoredoms</hi> (that is, their idolatries), but with <hi type="italic">their wickedness,</hi> or malice (<reference osisRef="Jer.3.2">v. 2</reference>), sins against the second table: for how can we think that those will be true to their neighbour that are false to their God? "Nay (<reference osisRef="Jer.3.5">v. 5</reference>), <hi type="italic">thou hast spoken and done evil things as thou couldst,</hi> and wouldst have spoken and done worse if thou hadst known how; thy will was to do it, but thou lackedst opportunity." Note, Those are wicked indeed that sin to the utmost of their power, that never refuse to comply with a temptation because they should not, but because they cannot. <div eID="gen17204" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17205" type="x-p"/> II. How gently God had corrected them for their sins. Instead of raining fire and brimstone upon them, because, like Sodom, they had <hi type="italic">avowed their sin</hi> and had gone after strange gods as Sodom after strange flesh, he only <hi type="italic">withheld the showers from them,</hi> and that only one part of the year: <hi type="italic">There has been no latter rain,</hi> which might serve as an intimation to them of their continual dependence upon God; when they had the former rain, that was no security to them for the latter, but they must still look up to God. But it had not this effect. <div eID="gen17205" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17206" type="x-p"/> III. How justly God might have abandoned them utterly, and refused ever to receive them again, though they should return; this would have been but according to the known rule of divorces, <reference osisRef="Jer.3.1">v. 1</reference>. <hi type="italic">They say</hi> (it is an adjudged case, nay, it is a case in which the law is very express, and it is what every body knows and speaks of, <reference osisRef="Deut.24.4">Deut. xxiv. 4</reference>), that if a woman be once put away for whoredom, and be joined to <hi type="italic">another man,</hi> her first husband shall never, upon any pretence whatsoever, take her again to be his wife; such playing fast and loose with the marriage-bond would be a horrid profanation of that ordinance and would <hi type="italic">greatly pollute that land.</hi> Observe, What the law says in this case—<hi type="italic">They say,</hi> that is, every one will say, and subscribe to the equity of the law in it; for every man finds something in himself that forbids him to entertain one that is <hi type="italic">another man's.</hi> And in like manner they had reason to expect that God would refuse ever to take them to be his people again, who had not only been joined to one strange god, but had <hi type="italic">played the harlot with many lovers.</hi> If we had to do with a man like ourselves, after such provocations as we have been guilty of, he would be implacable, and we might have despaired of his being reconciled to us. <div eID="gen17206" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17207" type="x-p"/> IV. How graciously he not only invites them, but directs them, to return to him. <div eID="gen17207" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17208" type="x-p"/> 1. He encourages them to hope that they shall find favour with him, upon their repentance: "Thou thou hast been bad, <hi type="italic">yet return again to me,</hi>" <reference osisRef="Jer.3.1">v. 1</reference>. This implies a promise that he will receive them: "Return, and thou shalt be welcome." God has not tied himself by the laws which he made for us, nor has he the peevish resentment that men have; he will be more kind to Israel, for the sake of his covenant with them, than ever any injured husband was to an adulterous wife; for in receiving penitents, as much as in any thing, he is <hi type="italic">God and not man.</hi> <div eID="gen17208" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17209" type="x-p"/> 2. He therefore kindly expects that they will repent and return to him, and he directs them what to say to him (<reference osisRef="Jer.3.4">v. 4</reference>): "<hi type="italic">Wilt thou not from this time cry unto me?</hi> Wilt not <hi type="italic">thou,</hi> who hast been in such relation to me, and on whom I have laid such obligations, <hi type="italic">wilt not thou cry to me?</hi> Though thou hast gone a whoring from me, yet, when thou findest the folly of it, surely thou wilt think of returning to me, now at least, now at last, in this thy day. Wilt thou not <hi type="italic">at this time,</hi> nay, wilt thou not <hi type="italic">from this time</hi> and forward, <hi type="italic">cry unto me?</hi> Whatever thou hast said or done hitherto, wilt thou not <hi type="italic">from this time</hi> apply to me? <hi type="italic">From this time</hi> of conviction and correction, now that thou hast been made to see thy sins (<reference osisRef="Jer.3.2">v. 2</reference>) and to smart for them (<reference osisRef="Jer.3.3">v. 3</reference>), wilt thou not now forsake them and return to me, saying, <hi type="italic">I will go and return to my first husband, for then it was better with me than now?</hi>" <reference osisRef="Hos.2.7">Hos. ii. 7</reference>. Or "<hi type="italic">from this time</hi> that thou hast had so kind an invitation to return, and assurance that thou shalt be well received: will not this grace of God overcome thee? Now that pardon is proclaimed wilt thou not come in and take the benefit of it? Surely thou wilt." <div eID="gen17209" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17210" type="x-p"/> (1.) He expects that they will claim relation to God, as theirs: <hi type="italic">Wilt thou not cry unto me, My Father, thou art the guide of my youth?</hi> [1.] They will surely come towards him as a father, to beg his pardon for their undutiful behaviour to him (<hi type="italic">Father, I have sinned</hi>) and will hope to find in him the tender compassions of a father towards a returning prodigal. They will come to him as a father, to whom they will make their complaints, and in whom they will put their confidence for relief and succour. They will now own him as their father, and themselves fatherless without him; and therefore, hoping to find mercy with him (as those penitents, <reference osisRef="Hos.14.3">Hos. xiv. 3</reference>), [2.] They will come to him as <hi type="italic">the guide of their youth,</hi> that is, as their husband, for so that relation is described, <reference osisRef="Mal.2.14">Mal. ii. 14</reference>. "Though thou hast gone after many lovers, surely thou wilt at length remember the love of thy espousals, and return to the <hi type="italic">husband of thy youth.</hi>" Or it may be taken more generally: "As <hi type="italic">my Father,</hi> thou <hi type="italic">art the guide of my youth.</hi>" Youth needs a guide. In our return to God we must thankfully remember that he <hi type="italic">was the guide of our youth</hi> in the way of comfort; and we must faithfully covenant that he shall be our guide henceforward in the way of duty, and that we will follow his guidance, and give up ourselves entirely to it, that in all doubtful cases we will be determined by our religion. <div eID="gen17210" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17211" type="x-p"/> (2.) He expects that they will appeal to the mercy of God and crave the benefit of that mercy (<reference osisRef="Jer.3.5">v. 5</reference>), that they will reason thus with themselves for their encouragement to return to him: "<hi type="italic">Will he reserve his anger for ever?</hi> Surely he will not, for he has proclaimed his name <hi type="italic">gracious and merciful.</hi>" Repenting sinners may encourage themselves with this, that, though God chide, he will not always chide, though he be angry, he will not keep his anger to the end, but, <hi type="italic">though he cause grief, he will have compassion,</hi> and may thus plead for reconciliation. Some understand this as describing their hypocrisy, and the impudence of it: "Though thou hast <hi type="italic">a whore's forehead</hi> (<reference osisRef="Jer.3.3">v. 3</reference>) and art still <hi type="italic">doing evil as thou canst</hi> (<reference osisRef="Jer.3.5">v. 5</reference>), yet art thou not ever and anon <hi type="italic">crying to me, My Father?</hi>" Even when they were most addicted to idols they pretended a regard to God and his service and kept up the forms of godliness and devotion. It is a shameful thing for men thus to call God father, and yet to do the <hi type="italic">works of the devil</hi> (as the Jews, <reference osisRef="John.8.44">John viii. 44</reference>), to call him the <hi type="italic">guide of their youth,</hi> and yet give up themselves to <hi type="italic">walk after the flesh,</hi> and to flatter themselves with the expectation that <hi type="italic">his anger shall have an end,</hi> while they are continually <hi type="italic">treasuring up to themselves wrath against the day of wrath.</hi>
entries.39e5b4ccedd943d3d2e6078b544d58b568b09dda: <div eID="gen17211" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Idolatries of Israel; The Treachery of Judah. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 620.)</title> <div sID="gen17212" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">6</hi> The <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> said also unto me in the days of Josiah the king, Hast thou seen <hi type="italic">that</hi> which backsliding Israel hath done? she is gone up upon every high mountain and under every green tree, and there hath played the harlot. <hi type="super">7</hi> And I said after she had done all these <hi type="italic">things,</hi> Turn thou unto me. But she returned not. And her treacherous sister Judah saw <hi type="italic">it.</hi> <hi type="super">8</hi> And I saw, when for all the causes whereby backsliding Israel committed adultery I had put her away, and given her a bill of divorce; yet her treacherous sister Judah feared not, but went and played the harlot also. <hi type="super">9</hi> And it came to pass through the lightness of her whoredom, that she defiled the land, and committed adultery with stones and with stocks. <hi type="super">10</hi> And yet for all this her treacherous sister Judah hath not turned unto me with her whole heart, but feignedly, saith the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> . <hi type="super">11</hi> And the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> said unto me, The backsliding Israel hath justified herself more than treacherous Judah. <div eID="gen17212" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17213" type="x-p"/> The date of this sermon must be observed, in order to the right understanding of it; it was <hi type="italic">in the days of Josiah,</hi> who set on foot a blessed work of reformation, in which he was hearty, but the people were not sincere in their compliance with it; to reprove them for that, and warn them of the consequences of their hypocrisy, is the scope of that which God here said to the prophet, and which he <hi type="italic">delivered to them.</hi> The case of the two kingdoms of Israel and Judah is here compared, the <hi type="italic">ten tribes</hi> that revolted from the throne of David and the temple of Jerusalem and the <hi type="italic">two tribes</hi> that adhered to both. The distinct history of those two kingdoms we have in the two books of the Kings, and here we have an abstract of both, as far as relates to this matter. <div eID="gen17213" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17214" type="x-p"/> I. Here is a short account of Israel, the ten tribes. Perhaps the prophet had been just reading the history of that kingdom when God came to him, and said, <hi type="italic">Hast thou seen what backsliding Israel has done?</hi> <reference osisRef="Jer.3.6">v. 6</reference>. For he could not see it otherwise than in history, they having been carried into captivity long before he was born. But what we read in the histories of scripture should instruct us and affect us, as if we ourselves had been eye-witnesses of it. She is called <hi type="italic">backsliding Israel</hi> because that kingdom was first founded in an apostasy from the divine institutions, both in church and state. Now he had seen concerning them, 1. That they were wretchedly addicted to idolatry. They had <hi type="italic">played the harlot upon every high mountain and under every green tree</hi> (<reference osisRef="Jer.3.6">v. 6</reference>), that is, they had worshipped other gods in their high places and groves; and no marvel, when from the first they had worshipped God by the images of the <hi type="italic">golden calves</hi> at Dan and Bethel. The way of idolatry is down-hill: those that are in love with images, and will have them, soon become in love with other gods, and will have them too; for how should those stick at the breach of the first commandment who make no conscience of the second? 2. That God by his prophets had invited and encouraged them to repent and reform (<reference osisRef="Jer.3.7">v. 7</reference>): "<hi type="italic">After she had done all these things,</hi> for which she might justly have been abandoned, yet <hi type="italic">I said</hi> unto her, <hi type="italic">Turn thou unto me</hi> and I will receive thee." Though they had forsaken both the house of David and the house of Aaron, who both had their authority <hi type="italic">jure divino—from God,</hi> without dispute, yet God sent his prophets among them, to call them to <hi type="italic">return to him,</hi> to the worship of him only, not insisting so much as one would have expected upon their return to the house of David, but pressing their return to the house of Aaron. We read not that Elijah, that great reformer, ever mentioned their return to the house of David, while he was anxious for their return to the faithful service of the true God according as they had it among them. It is serious piety that God stands upon more than even his own rituals. 3. That, notwithstanding this, they had persisted in their idolatries: <hi type="italic">But she returned not,</hi> and God <hi type="italic">saw it;</hi> he took notice of it, and was much displeased with it, <reference osisRef="Jer.3.7-Jer.3.8">v. 7, 8</reference>. Note, God keeps account, whether we do or no, how often he has called to us to turn to him and we have refused. 4. That he had therefore cast them off, and given them up into the hands of their enemies (<reference osisRef="Jer.3.8">v. 8</reference>): <hi type="italic">When I saw</hi> (so it may be read) <hi type="italic">that for all the actions wherein she had committed adultery I must dismiss her, I gave her a bill of divorce.</hi> God divorced them when he threw them out of his protection and left them an easy prey to any that would lay hands on them, when he scattered all their synagogues and the schools of the prophets and excluded them from laying any further claim to the covenant made with their fathers. Note, Those will justly be divorced from God that join themselves to such as are rivals with him. For proof of this go and see what God did to Israel. <div eID="gen17214" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17215" type="x-p"/> II. Let us now see what was the case of Judah, the kingdom of the two tribes. She is called <hi type="italic">treacherous sister Judah,</hi> a sister because descended from the same common stock, Abraham and Jacob; but, as Israel had the character of a <hi type="italic">backslider,</hi> So Judah is called <hi type="italic">treacherous,</hi> because, though she professed to keep close to God when Israel had backslidden (she adhered to the kings and priests that were of God's own appointing, and did not withdraw from her allegiance, so that it was expected she should deal faithfully), yet she proved treacherous, and false, and unfaithful to her professions and promises. Note, The treachery of those who pretend to cleave to God will be reckoned for, as well as the apostasy of those who openly revolt from him. Judah saw what Israel did, and what came of it, and should have taken warning. Israel's captivity was intended for Judah's admonition; but it had not the designed effect. Judah feared not, but thought herself safe because she had Levites to be her priests and sons of David to be her kings. Note, It is an evidence of great stupidity and security when we are not awakened to a holy fear by the judgments of God upon others. It is here charged on Judah, 1. That when they had a wicked king that debauched them they heartily concurred with him in his debaucheries. Judah was forward enough to <hi type="italic">play the harlot,</hi> to worship any idol that was introduced among them and to join in any idolatrous usage; so that <hi type="italic">through the lightness</hi> (or, as some read it, the <hi type="italic">vileness</hi> and <hi type="italic">baseness) of her whoredom,</hi> or (as the margin reads it) by the fame and <hi type="italic">report</hi> of her whoredom, her <hi type="italic">notorious</hi> whoredom, for which she had become infamous, she <hi type="italic">defiled the land,</hi> and made it an abomination to God; for she <hi type="italic">committed adultery with stones and stocks,</hi> with the basest idols, those made of <hi type="italic">wood and stone.</hi> In the reigns of Manasseh and Amon, when they were disposed to idolatry, the people were so too, and all the country was corrupted with it, and none feared the ruin which Israel by this means had brought upon themselves. 2. That when they had a good king, that reformed them, they did not heartily concur with him in the reformation. This was the present case. God tried whether they would be good in a good reign, but the evil disposition was still the same: <hi type="italic">They returned not to me with their whole heart, but feignedly,</hi> <reference osisRef="Jer.3.10">v. 10</reference>. Josiah went further in destroying idolatry than the best of his predecessors had done, and for his own part he <hi type="italic">turned to the Lord with all his heart and with all his soul;</hi> so it is said of him, <reference osisRef="2Kgs.23.25">2 Kings xxiii. 25</reference>. The people were forced to an external compliance with him, and joined with him in keeping a very solemn passover and in renewing their covenants with God (<reference osisRef="2Chr.34.32">2 Chron. xxxiv. 32</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Chr.35.17">xxxv. 17</reference>); but they were not sincere in it, nor were their <hi type="italic">hearts right with God.</hi> For this reason God at that very time said, <hi type="italic">I will remove Judah out of my sight, as I removed Israel</hi> (<reference osisRef="2Kgs.23.27">2 Kings xxiii. 27</reference>), because Judah was not removed from their sin by the sight of Israel's removal from their land. Hypocritical and ineffectual reformations bode ill to a people. We deceive ourselves if we think to deceive God by a feigned return to him. I know no religion without sincerity. <div eID="gen17215" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17216" type="x-p"/> III. The case of these sister kingdoms is compared, and judgment given upon the comparison, that of the two Judah was the worse (<reference osisRef="Jer.3.11">v. 11</reference>): <hi type="italic">Israel has justified herself more than Judah,</hi> that is, she is not so bad as Judah is. This comparative justification will stand Israel in little stead; what will it avail us to say, <hi type="italic">We are not so bad as others,</hi> when yet we are not really good ourselves? But it will serve as an aggravation of the sin of Judah, which was in two respects worse than that of Israel:—1. More was expected from Judah than from Israel; so that Judah dealt treacherously, they vilified a more sacred profession, and falsified a more solemn promise, than Israel did. 2. Judah might have taken warning by the ruin of Israel for their idolatry, and would not. God's judgments upon others, if they be not means of our reformation, will help to aggravate our destruction. The prophet Ezekiel (<reference osisRef="Jer.23.11">ch. xxiii. 11</reference>) makes the same comparison between Jerusalem and Samaria that this prophet here makes between Judah and Israel, nay, and (<reference osisRef="Ezek.16.48">Ezek. xvi. 48</reference>) between Jerusalem and Sodom, and Jerusalem is made the worst of the three.
entries.002a7e2c935c4615c8bf30f873bcabf117572545: <div eID="gen17216" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Encouragements to Repentance. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 620.)</title> <div sID="gen17217" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">12</hi> Go and proclaim these words toward the north, and say, Return, thou backsliding Israel, saith the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> ; <hi type="italic">and</hi> I will not cause mine anger to fall upon you: for I <hi type="italic">am</hi> merciful, saith the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , <hi type="italic">and</hi> I will not keep <hi type="italic">anger</hi> for ever. <hi type="super">13</hi> Only acknowledge thine iniquity, that thou hast transgressed against the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> thy God, and hast scattered thy ways to the strangers under every green tree, and ye have not obeyed my voice, saith the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> . <hi type="super">14</hi> Turn, O backsliding children, saith the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> ; for I am married unto you: and I will take you one of a city, and two of a family, and I will bring you to Zion: <hi type="super">15</hi> And I will give you pastors according to mine heart, which shall feed you with knowledge and understanding. <hi type="super">16</hi> And it shall come to pass, when ye be multiplied and increased in the land, in those days, saith the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , they shall say no more, The ark of the covenant of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> : neither shall it come to mind: neither shall they remember it; neither shall they visit <hi type="italic">it;</hi> neither shall <hi type="italic">that</hi> be done any more. <hi type="super">17</hi> At that time they shall call Jerusalem the throne of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> ; and all the nations shall be gathered unto it, to the name of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , to Jerusalem: neither shall they walk any more after the imagination of their evil heart. <hi type="super">18</hi> In those days the house of Judah shall walk with the house of Israel, and they shall come together out of the land of the north to the land that I have given for an inheritance unto your fathers. <hi type="super">19</hi> But I said, How shall I put thee among the children, and give thee a pleasant land, a goodly heritage of the hosts of nations? and I said, Thou shalt call me, My father; and shalt not turn away from me. <div eID="gen17217" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17218" type="x-p"/> Here is a great deal of gospel in these verses, both that which was always gospel, God's readiness to pardon sin and to receive and entertain returning repenting sinners, and those blessings which were in a special manner reserved for gospel times, the forming and founding of the gospel church by bringing into it the <hi type="italic">children of God that were scattered abroad,</hi> the superseding of the ceremonial law, and the uniting of Jews and Gentiles, typified by the uniting of Israel and Judah in their return out of captivity. The prophet is directed to <hi type="italic">proclaim these words towards the north,</hi> for they are a call to backsliding Israel, the ten tribes that were carried captive into Assyria, which lay north from Jerusalem. That way he must look, to show that God had not forgotten them, though their brethren had, and to upbraid the men of Judah with their obstinacy in refusing to answer the calls given them. One might as well call to those who lay many hundred miles off in the land of the north; they would as soon hear as these unbelieving and disobedient people; <hi type="italic">backsliding Israel</hi> will sooner accept of mercy, and have the benefit of it, than <hi type="italic">treacherous Judah.</hi> And perhaps the proclaiming of these words towards the north looks as far forward as the <hi type="italic">preaching of repentance and remission of sins unto all nations, beginning at Jerusalem,</hi> <reference osisRef="Luke.24.47">Luke xxiv. 47</reference>. A call to Israel in the land of the north is a call to others in that land, even as many as belong to the election of grace. When it was suspected that Christ would <hi type="italic">go to the dispersed</hi> Jews among the Gentiles, it was concluded that he would <hi type="italic">teach the Gentiles,</hi> <reference osisRef="John.7.35">John vii. 35</reference>. So here. <div eID="gen17218" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17219" type="x-p"/> I. Here is an invitation given to <hi type="italic">backsliding Israel,</hi> and in them to the backsliding Gentiles, to <hi type="italic">return unto God,</hi> the God from whom they had revolted (<reference osisRef="Jer.3.12">v. 12</reference>): <hi type="italic">Return, thou backsliding Israel.</hi> And again (<reference osisRef="Jer.3.14">v. 14</reference>): "<hi type="italic">Turn, O backsliding children!</hi> repent of your backslidings, return to your allegiance, come back to that good way which you have missed and out of which you have turned aside." Pursuant to this invitation, 1. They are encouraged to return. "<hi type="italic">Repent, and be converted, and your sins shall be blotted out,</hi> <reference osisRef="Acts.3.19">Acts iii. 19</reference>. You have incurred God's displeasure, but return to me, and <hi type="italic">I will not cause my anger to fall upon you.</hi>" God's anger is ready to fall upon sinners, as a lion falls on his prey, and there is none to deliver, as a mountain of lead falling on them, to sink them past recovery into the lowest hell. But if they repent it shall be turned away, <reference osisRef="Isa.12.1">Isa. xii. 1</reference>. <hi type="italic">I will not keep my anger for ever,</hi> but will be reconciled, <hi type="italic">for I am merciful.</hi> We that are sinful were for ever undone if God were not merciful; but the goodness of his nature encourages us to hope that, if we by repentance undo what we have done against him, he will by a pardon unsay what he has said against us. 2. They are directed how to return (<reference osisRef="Jer.3.13">v. 13</reference>): "<hi type="italic">Only acknowledge thy iniquity,</hi> own thyself in a fault and thereby take shame to thyself and give glory to God." <hi type="italic">I will not keep my anger for ever</hi> (that is a previous promise); you shall be delivered form that anger of God which is everlasting, from the wrath to come; but upon what terms? Very easy and reasonable ones. <hi type="italic">Only acknowledge thy sins. If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive them.</hi> This will aggravate the condemnation of sinners, that the terms of pardon and peace were brought so low, and yet they would not come up to them. <hi type="italic">If the prophet had told thee to do some great thing wouldst thou not have done it? How much more when he says, Only acknowledge thy iniquity?</hi> <reference osisRef="2Kgs.5.13">2 Kings v. 13</reference>. In confessing sin, (1.) We must own the corruption of our nature: <hi type="italic">Acknowledge thy iniquity,</hi> the perverseness and irregularity of thy nature. (2.) We must own our actual sins: "<hi type="italic">That thou hast transgressed against the Lord thy God,</hi> hast affronted him and offended him." (3.) We must own the multitude of our transgressions: "That <hi type="italic">thou hast scattered thy ways to the strangers,</hi> run hither and thither in pursuit of thy idols, <hi type="italic">under every green tree.</hi> Wherever thou hast rambled thou hast left behind thee the marks of thy folly." (4.) We must aggravate our sin from the disobedience that there is in it to the divine law. The sinfulness of sin is the worst thing in it: "<hi type="italic">You have not obeyed my voice;</hi> acknowledge that, and let that humble you more than any thing else." <div eID="gen17219" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17220" type="x-p"/> II. Here are precious promises made to these backsliding children, if they do return, which were in part fulfilled in the return of the Jews out of their captivity, many that belonged to the ten tribes having perhaps joined themselves to those of the two tribes, in the prospect of their deliverance, and returning with them; but the prophecy is to have its full accomplishment in the gospel church, and the gathering together of <hi type="italic">the children of God that were scattered abroad</hi> to that: "Return, for, though you are backsliders, yet you are children; nay, though a treacherous wife, yet a wife, for <hi type="italic">I am married to you</hi> (<reference osisRef="Jer.3.14">v. 14</reference>) and will not disown the relation." Thus God remembers his covenant with their fathers, that marriage covenant, and in consideration of that he <hi type="italic">remembers their land,</hi> <reference osisRef="Lev.26.42">Lev. xxvi. 42</reference>. <div eID="gen17220" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17221" type="x-p"/> 1. He promises to gather them together from all places whither they are dispersed and scattered abroad, <reference osisRef="John.11.52">John xi. 52</reference>, <hi type="italic">I will take you, one of a city, and two of a family,</hi> or clan; <hi type="italic">and I will bring you to Zion,</hi> <reference osisRef="Jer.3.14">v. 14</reference>. All those that by repentance return to their duty shall return to their former comfort. Observe, (1.) God will graciously receive those that return to him, nay, it is he that by his distinguishing grace takes them out from among the rest that persist in their backslidings; if he had left them, they would have been undone. (2.) Of the many that have backslidden from God there are but few, very few in comparison, that return to him, like the gleanings of the vintage—<hi type="italic">one of a city and two of a country;</hi> Christ's flock is a little flock, and <hi type="italic">few there are that find the strait gate.</hi> (3.) Of those few, though dispersed, yet not one shall be lost. Though there be but <hi type="italic">one in a city,</hi> God will find out that one; he shall not be overlooked in a crowd, but shall be brought safely to Zion, safely to heaven. The scattered Jews shall be brought to Jerusalem, and those of the ten tribes shall be as welcome there as those of the two. God's chosen, scattered all the world over, shall be brought to <hi type="italic">the gospel church,</hi> that Mount Zion, the heavenly Jerusalem, that holy hill on which Christ reigns. <div eID="gen17221" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17222" type="x-p"/> 2. He promises to set those over them that shall be every way blessings to them (<reference osisRef="Jer.3.15">v. 15</reference>): <hi type="italic">I will give you pastors after my heart,</hi> alluding to the character given of David when God pitched upon him to be king. <reference osisRef="1Sam.13.14">1 Sam. xiii. 14</reference>, <hi type="italic">The Lord hath sought him a man after his own heart.</hi> Observe, (1.) When a church is gathered it must be governed. "<hi type="italic">I will bring them to Zion,</hi> not to live as they list, but to be under discipline, not as wild beasts, that range at pleasure, but as sheep that are under the direction of a shepherd." <hi type="italic">I will give them pastors,</hi> that is, both magistrates and ministers; both are God's ordinance for the support of his kingdom. (2.) It is well with a people when their pastors are <hi type="italic">after God's own heart,</hi> such as they should be, such as we would have them be, who shall make his will their rule in all their administrations, and such as endeavour in some measure to conform to his example, who rule for him, and, as they are capable, rule like him. (3.) Those are pastors after God's own heart who make it their business to feed the flock, not to <hi type="italic">feed themselves and fleece the flocks,</hi> but to do all they can for the good of those that are under their charge, who <hi type="italic">feed them with wisdom and understanding</hi> (that is, wisely and understandingly), as David fed them, in the <hi type="italic">integrity of his heart</hi> and by the <hi type="italic">skilfulness of his hand,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.78.72">Ps. lxxviii. 72</reference>. Those who are not only pastors, but teachers, must feed them with the word of God, which is wisdom and understanding, which is able to make us wise to salvation. <div eID="gen17222" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17223" type="x-p"/> 3. He promises that there shall be no more occasion for the <hi type="italic">ark of the covenant,</hi> which had been so much the glory of the tabernacle first and afterwards of the temple, and was the token of God's presence with them; that shall be set aside, and there shall be no more enquiry after, nor enquiring of, it (<reference osisRef="Jer.3.16">v. 16</reference>): <hi type="italic">When you shall be multiplied and increased in the land,</hi> when the kingdom of the Messiah shall be set up, which by the accession of the Gentiles will bring in to the church a vast increase (and the days of the Messiah the Jewish masters themselves acknowledge to be here intended), then <hi type="italic">they shall say no more, The ark of the covenant of the Lord,</hi> they shall have it no more among them to value, or value themselves upon, because they shall have a pure spiritual way of worship set up, in which there shall be no occasion for any of those external ordinances; with the <hi type="italic">ark of the covenant</hi> the whole ceremonial law shall be set aside, and all the institutions of it, for Christ, the truth of all those types, exhibited to us in the word and sacraments of the New Testament, will be to us instead of all. It is very likely (whatever the Jews suggest to the contrary) that <hi type="italic">the ark of the covenant</hi> was in the second temple, being restored by Cyrus with the other <hi type="italic">vessels of the house of the Lord,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ezra.1.7">Ezra i. 7</reference>. But in the gospel temple Christ <hi type="italic">is the ark;</hi> he is the propitiatory, or mercy-seat; and it is the spiritual presence of God in his ordinances that we are now to expect. Many expressions are here used concerning the setting aside of the ark, that it shall not <hi type="italic">come to mind,</hi> that they <hi type="italic">shall not remember it,</hi> that they shall <hi type="italic">not visit it,</hi> that none of these things shall be <hi type="italic">any more done;</hi> for the <hi type="italic">true worshippers shall worship the Father in spirit and in truth,</hi> <reference osisRef="John.4.24">John iv. 24</reference>. But this variety of expressions is used to show that the ceremonies of the law of Moses should be totally and finally abolished, never to be used any more, but that it would be with difficulty that those who had been so long wedded to them should be weaned from them; and that they would not quite let them go till their holy city and holy house should both be levelled with the ground. <div eID="gen17223" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17224" type="x-p"/> 4. He promises that the gospel church, here called <hi type="italic">Jerusalem,</hi> shall become eminent and conspicuous, <reference osisRef="Jer.3.17">v. 17</reference>. Two things shall make it famous:—(1.) God's special residence and dominion in it. It shall be called, <hi type="italic">The throne of the Lord</hi>—the throne of <hi type="italic">his glory,</hi> for that shines forth in the church—the throne of <hi type="italic">his government,</hi> for that also is erected there; there he rules his willing people by his word and Spirit, and brings every thought into obedience to himself. As the gospel got ground this <hi type="italic">throne of the Lord</hi> was set up even where <hi type="italic">Satan's seat</hi> had been. It is especially the throne of <hi type="italic">his grace;</hi> for those that by faith come to this Jerusalem come to <hi type="italic">God the judge of all,</hi> and to <hi type="italic">Jesus the mediator of the new covenant,</hi> <reference osisRef="Heb.12.22-Heb.12.24">Heb. xii. 22-24</reference>. (2.) The accession of the Gentiles to it. <hi type="italic">All the nations shall be</hi> discipled, and so <hi type="italic">gathered</hi> to the church, and shall become subjects to that <hi type="italic">throne of the Lord</hi> which is there set up, and devoted to the honour of that <hi type="italic">name of the Lord</hi> which is there both manifested and called upon. <div eID="gen17224" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17225" type="x-p"/> 5. He promises that there shall be a wonderful reformation wrought in those that are gathered to the church: <hi type="italic">They shall not walk any more after the imagination of their evil hearts.</hi> They shall not live as they list, but live by rules, not do according to their own corrupt appetites, but according to the will of God. See what leads in sin—<hi type="italic">the imagination of our own evil hearts;</hi> and what sin is—it is <hi type="italic">walking after</hi> that imagination, being governed by fancy and humour; and what converting grace does—it takes us off from walking after <hi type="italic">our own inventions</hi> and brings us to be governed by religion and right reason. <div eID="gen17225" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17226" type="x-p"/> 6. That Judah and Israel shall be happily united in one body, <reference osisRef="Jer.3.18">v. 18</reference>. They were so in their return out of captivity and their settlement again in Canaan: <hi type="italic">The house of Judah shall walk with the house of Israel,</hi> as being perfectly agreed, and become <hi type="italic">one stick in the hand of the Lord,</hi> as Ezekiel also foretold, <reference osisRef="Jer.37.16-Jer.37.17">ch. xxxvii. 16, 17</reference>. Both Assyria and Chaldea fell into the hands of Cyrus, and his proclamation extended to all the Jews in all his dominions. And therefore we have reason to think that many of <hi type="italic">the house of Israel</hi> came with those of Judah out of <hi type="italic">the land of the north;</hi> though at first there returned but 42,000 (whom we have an account of, <reference osisRef="Ezra.2.1-Ezra.2.70">Ezra ii.</reference>) yet Josephus says (<hi type="italic">Antiq.</hi> 11.68) that some few years after, under Darius, Zerubbabel went and fetched up above 4,000 000 of souls, <hi type="italic">to the land that was given for an inheritance to their fathers.</hi> And we never read of such animosities and enmities between Israel and Judah as had been formerly. This happy coalescence between Israel and Judah in Canaan was a type of the uniting of Jews and Gentiles in the gospel church, when, all enmities being slain, they should become one <hi type="italic">sheepfold under one shepherd.</hi> <div eID="gen17226" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17227" type="x-p"/> III. Here is some difficulty started, that lies in the way of all this mercy; but an expedient is found to get over it. <div eID="gen17227" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17228" type="x-p"/> 1. God asks, <hi type="italic">How shall I</hi> do this for thee? Not as if God showed favour with reluctancy, as he punishes with a <hi type="italic">How shall I give thee up?</hi> <reference osisRef="Hos.11.8-Hos.11.9">Hos. xi. 8, 9</reference>. No, though he is slow to anger, he is swift to show mercy. But it intimates that we are utterly unworthy of his favours, that we have no reason to expect them, that there is nothing in us to deserve them, that we can lay no claim to them, and that he contrives how to do it in such a way as may save the honour of his justice and holiness in the government of the world. <hi type="italic">Means</hi> must be <hi type="italic">devised that his banished be not for ever expelled from him,</hi> <reference osisRef="2Sam.14.14">2 Sam. xiv. 14</reference>. How shall I do it? (1.) Even backsliders, if they return and repent, shall be <hi type="italic">put among the children;</hi> and who could ever have expected that? <hi type="italic">Behold what manner of love is this!</hi> <reference osisRef="1John.3.1">1 John iii. 1</reference>. How should we who are so mean and weak, so worthless and unworthy, and so provoking, ever be <hi type="italic">put among the children.</hi> (2.) To those whom God puts among the children he will <hi type="italic">give the pleasant land,</hi> the land of Canaan, that glory of all lands, <hi type="italic">that goodly heritage of the hosts of nations,</hi> which nations and their hosts wish for and prefer to their own country, or which the hosts of the nations have now got possession of. It was a type of heaven, where there are <hi type="italic">pleasures for evermore.</hi> Now who could expect a place in that <hi type="italic">pleasant land</hi> that has so often <hi type="italic">despised it</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ps.106.24">Ps. cvi. 24</reference>) and is so unworthy of it and unfit for it? Is this the manner of men? <div eID="gen17228" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17229" type="x-p"/> 2. He does himself return answer to this question: <hi type="italic">But I said, Thou shalt call me, My Father.</hi> God does himself answer all the objections that are taken from our unworthiness, or they would never be got over. (1.) That he may put returning penitents <hi type="italic">among the children,</hi> he will give them the <hi type="italic">Spirit of adoption,</hi> teaching them <hi type="italic">to cry, Abba, Father,</hi> <reference osisRef="Gal.4.6">Gal. iv. 6</reference>. "<hi type="italic">Thou shalt call me, My Father;</hi> thou shalt return to me, and resign thyself to me as a father, and that shall recommend thee to my favour," (2.) That he may <hi type="italic">give them the pleasant land,</hi> he will <hi type="italic">put his fear in their hearts,</hi> that they may never <hi type="italic">turn from him,</hi> but may persevere to the end.
entries.21ec987205bae581152b6b2b54106b6d9c19e3de: <div eID="gen17229" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Israel Returning to God; Israel Encouraged in Their Return. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 620.)</title> <div sID="gen17230" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">20</hi> Surely <hi type="italic">as</hi> a wife treacherously departeth from her husband, so have ye dealt treacherously with me, O house of Israel, saith the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> . <hi type="super">21</hi> A voice was heard upon the high places, weeping <hi type="italic">and</hi> supplications of the children of Israel: for they have perverted their way, <hi type="italic">and</hi> they have forgotten the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> their God. <hi type="super">22</hi> Return, ye backsliding children, <hi type="italic">and</hi> I will heal your backslidings. Behold, we come unto thee; for thou <hi type="italic">art</hi> the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> our God. <hi type="super">23</hi> Truly in vain <hi type="italic">is salvation hoped for</hi> from the hills, <hi type="italic">and from</hi> the multitude of mountains: truly in the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> our God <hi type="italic">is</hi> the salvation of Israel. <hi type="super">24</hi> For shame hath devoured the labour of our fathers from our youth; their flocks and their herds, their sons and their daughters. <hi type="super">25</hi> We lie down in our shame, and our confusion covereth us: for we have sinned against the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> our God, we and our fathers, from our youth even unto this day, and have not obeyed the voice of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> our God. <div eID="gen17230" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17231" type="x-p"/> Here is, I. The charge God exhibits against Israel for their treacherous departures from him, <reference osisRef="Jer.3.20">v. 20</reference>. As an adulterous wife elopes from her husband, so have they gone a whoring from God. They were joined to God by a marriage-covenant, but they broke that covenant, they <hi type="italic">dealt treacherously</hi> with God, who had always dealt kindly and faithfully with them. Treacherous dealing with men like ourselves is bad enough, but to deal treacherously with God is to deal treasonably. <div eID="gen17231" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17232" type="x-p"/> II. Their conviction and confession of the truth of this charge, <reference osisRef="Jer.3.21">v. 21</reference>. When God reproved them for their apostasy, there were some among them, even such as God would take and <hi type="italic">bring to Zion,</hi> whose <hi type="italic">voice was heard upon the high places weeping and praying,</hi> humbling themselves before the God of their fathers, lamenting their calamities, and their sins, the procuring cause of them; for this is that which they lament, for this they bemoan themselves, that <hi type="italic">they have perverted their way and forgotten the Lord their God.</hi> Note, 1. Sin is the perverting of our way, it is turning aside to crooked ways and <hi type="italic">perverting that which is right.</hi> 2. Forgetting the Lord our God is at the bottom of all sin. If men would remember God, his eye upon them and their obligation to him, they would not transgress as they do. 3. By sin we embarrass ourselves, and bring ourselves into trouble, for that also is the perverting of our way, <reference osisRef="Lam.3.9">Lam. iii. 9</reference>. 4. Prayers and tears well become those whose consciences tell them that they have <hi type="italic">perverted their way and forgotten their God.</hi> When the <hi type="italic">foolishness of man perverts his way his heart</hi> is apt to <hi type="italic">fret against the Lord</hi> (<reference osisRef="Prov.19.3">Prov. xix. 3</reference>), whereas it should be melted and poured out before him. <div eID="gen17232" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17233" type="x-p"/> III. The invitation God gives them to return to him (<reference osisRef="Jer.3.22">v. 22</reference>): <hi type="italic">Return, you backsliding children.</hi> He calls them <hi type="italic">children</hi> in tenderness and compassion to them, foolish and froward as children, yet <hi type="italic">his sons,</hi> whom though he corrects he will not disinherit; for, though they are <hi type="italic">refractory children</hi> (so some render it), yet they are <hi type="italic">children.</hi> God bears with such children, and so much parents. When they are convinced of sin (<reference osisRef="Jer.3.21">v. 21</reference>), and humbled for that, then they are prepared and then they are <hi type="italic">invited</hi> to <hi type="italic">return,</hi> as Christ invites those to him that are <hi type="italic">weary</hi> and <hi type="italic">heavy-laden.</hi> The promise to those that return is, "<hi type="italic">I will heal your backslidings;</hi> I will comfort you under the grief you are in for your backslidings, deliver you out of the troubles you have brought yourselves into by your backslidings, and cure you of your refractoriness and tendency to backslide." God will <hi type="italic">heal our backslidings</hi> by his pardoning mercy, his quieting peace, and his renewing grace. <div eID="gen17233" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17234" type="x-p"/> IV. The ready consent they give to this invitation, and their cheerful compliance with it: <hi type="italic">Behold, we come unto thee.</hi> This is an echo to God's call; as a voice returned from broken walls, so this from broken hearts. God says, <hi type="italic">Return;</hi> they answer, <hi type="italic">Behold, we come.</hi> It is an immediate speedy answer, without delay, not, "We will come hereafter," but, "We do come now; we need not take time to consider of it;" not, "We come towards thee," but, "We come to thee, we will make a thorough turn of it." Observe how unanimous they are: <hi type="italic">We come,</hi> one and all. 1. They come devoting themselves to God as theirs: "<hi type="italic">Thou art the Lord our God;</hi> we take thee to be ours, we give up ourselves to thee to be thine; whither shall we go but to thee? It is our sin and folly that we have gone from thee." It is very comfortable, in our returns to God after our backslidings, to look up to him as ours in covenant. 2. They come disclaiming all expectations of relief and succour but from God only: <hi type="italic">"In vain is salvation hoped for from the hills and from the multitude of the mountains;</hi> we now see our folly in relying upon creature-confidences, and will never so deceive ourselves any more." They worshipped their idols upon hills and mountains (<reference osisRef="Jer.3.6">v. 6</reference>), and they had a multitude of idols upon their mountains, which they had sought unto and put a confidence in; but now they will have no more to do with them. In vain do we look for any thing that is good from them, while from God we may look for every thing that is good, even salvation itself. Therefore, 3. They come depending upon God only as their God: <hi type="italic">In the Lord our God is the salvation of Israel.</hi> He is <hi type="italic">the Lord,</hi> and he only can save; he can save when all other succours and saviours fail; and he is <hi type="italic">our God,</hi> and will in his own way and time work salvation for us. It is very applicable to the great salvation from sin, which Jesus Christ wrought out for us; that is the <hi type="italic">salvation of the Lord,</hi> his <hi type="italic">great salvation.</hi> 4. They come justifying God in their troubles and judging themselves for their sins, <reference osisRef="Jer.3.24-Jer.3.25">v. 24, 25</reference>. (1.) They impute all the calamities they had been under to their idols, which had not only done them no good, but had done them abundance of mischief, all the mischief that had been done them: <hi type="italic">Shame</hi> (the idol, that shameful thing) <hi type="italic">has devoured the labour of our fathers.</hi> Note, [1.] True penitents have learned to call sin <hi type="italic">shame;</hi> even the beloved sin which has been as an idol to them, which they have been most pleased with and proud of, even that they shall call a scandalous thing, shall put contempt upon it and be ashamed of it. [2.] True penitents have learned to call sin death and ruin, and to charge upon it all the mischiefs they suffer: "It has <hi type="italic">devoured</hi> all those good things which our fathers <hi type="italic">laboured for</hi> and left to us; we have found <hi type="italic">from our youth</hi> that our idolatry has been the destruction of our prosperity." Children often throw away upon their lusts that which their fathers took a great deal of pains for; and it is well if at length they are brought (as these here) to see the folly of it, and to call those vices their shame which have wasted their estates and <hi type="italic">devoured the labour of their fathers.</hi> Of the labour of their fathers, which their idols had devoured, they mention particularly <hi type="italic">their flocks and their herds, their sons and their daughters. First,</hi> their idolatries had provoked God to bring these desolating judgments upon them, which had ruined their country and families, and made their estates a prey and their children captives to the conquering enemy. They had <hi type="italic">procured these things to themselves.</hi> Or, rather, <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> These had been sacrificed to their idols, had been <hi type="italic">separated unto that shame</hi> (<reference osisRef="Hos.9.10">Hos. ix. 10</reference>), and they had devoured them without mercy; they did <hi type="italic">eat the fat of their sacrifices</hi> (<reference osisRef="Deut.32.38">Deut. xxxii. 38</reference>), even their human sacrifices. (2.) They take to themselves the shame of their sin and folly (<reference osisRef="Jer.3.25">v. 25</reference>): "<hi type="italic">We lie down in our shame,</hi> being unable to bear up under it; <hi type="italic">our confusion covers us,</hi> that is, both our penal and our penitential shame. Sin has laid us under such rebukes of God's providence, and such reproaches of our own consciences, as surround us and fill us with shame. For <hi type="italic">we have sinned,</hi> and shame came in with sin and still attends upon it. We are sinners by descent; guilt and corruption are entailed upon us: <hi type="italic">We and our fathers have sinned.</hi> We were sinners betimes; we began early in a course of sin: We have sinned <hi type="italic">from our youth;</hi> we have continued in sin, have sinned <hi type="italic">even unto this day,</hi> though often called to repent and forsake our sins. That which is the malignity of sin, the worst thing in it, is the affront we have put upon God by it: <hi type="italic">We have not obeyed the voice of the Lord our God,</hi> forbidding us to sin and commanding us, when we have sinned, to repent." Now all this seems to be the language of the penitents of <hi type="italic">the house of Israel</hi> (<reference osisRef="Jer.3.20">v. 20</reference>), of the ten tribes, either of those that were in captivity or those of them that remained in their own land. And the prophet takes notice of their repentance to provoke the men of Judah to a holy emulation. David used it as an argument with the elders of Judah that it would be a shame for those that were <hi type="italic">his bone and his flesh</hi> to be <hi type="italic">the last in bringing the king back,</hi> when the men of Israel appeared forward in it, <reference osisRef="2Sam.19.11-2Sam.19.12">2 Sam. xix. 11, 12</reference>. So the prophet excites Judah to repent because Israel did: and well it were if the zeal of others less likely would provoke us to strive to get before them and go beyond them in that which is good.  <chapter eID="Jer.3"/> <div eID="gen17234" type="x-p"/>

entries.f48f5a0ed5ce0b17e4eb35d08501f488922b2bf2: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv9626"/><title type="x-s2">CHAPTER 3</title> <title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Jer.3.1-Jer.3.25">Jr 3:1-25</reference>. God's Mercy notwithstanding Judah's Vileness.</title> <div sID="gen16952" type="x-p"/> Contrary to all precedent in the case of adultery, Jehovah offers a return to Judah, the spiritual adulteress (<reference osisRef="Jer.3.1-Jer.3.5">Jr 3:1-5</reference>). A new portion of the book, ending with the sixth chapter. Judah worse than Israel; yet both shall be restored in the last days (<reference osisRef="Jer.3.6-Jer.3.25">Jr 3:6-25</reference>).<div eID="gen16952" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16953" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv9626"/><hi type="bold">1. They say--</hi>rather, as Hebrew, "saying," in agreement with "the Lord"; <reference osisRef="Jer.2.37">Jr 2:37</reference> of last chapter [Maurer]. Or, it is equivalent to, "Suppose this case." Some copyist may have omitted, "The word of the Lord came to me," saying.<div eID="gen16953" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16954" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">shall he return unto her--</hi>will he take her back? It was unlawful to do so (<reference osisRef="Deut.24.1-Deut.24.4">De 24:1-4</reference>).<div eID="gen16954" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16955" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">shall not--</hi>Should not the land be polluted if this were done?<div eID="gen16955" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16956" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">yet return--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Jer.3.22">Jr 3:22</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.4.1">Jr 4:1</reference>; <reference osisRef="Zech.1.3">Zec 1:3</reference>; compare <reference osisRef="Ezek.16.51">Eze 16:51</reference>, 58, 60). "Nevertheless," &c. (see on <reference osisRef="Isa.50.1">Is 50:1</reference>). <div eID="gen16956" type="x-p"/>
entries.e610d3536981c47bc4e64ccaafd29d5520b54495: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv9627"/><div sID="gen16957" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv9627"/><hi type="bold">2. high places--</hi>the scene of idolatries which were spiritual adulteries.<div eID="gen16957" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16958" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">In ... ways ... sat for them--</hi>watching for lovers like a prostitute (<reference osisRef="Gen.38.14">Ge 38:14</reference>, <reference osisRef="Gen.38.21">21</reference>; <reference osisRef="Prov.7.12">Pr 7:12</reference>; <reference osisRef="Prov.23.28">23:28</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ezek.16.24">Eze 16:24</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ezek.16.25">25</reference>), and like an Arab who lies in wait for travellers. The Arabs of the desert, east and south of Palestine, are still notorious as robbers. <div eID="gen16958" type="x-p"/>
entries.e914eeddb787a12d4ceb108dd98e5b7468626863: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv9628"/><div sID="gen16959" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv9628"/><hi type="bold">3. no latter rain--</hi>essential to the crops in Palestine; withheld in judgment (<reference osisRef="Lev.26.19">Le 26:19</reference>; compare <reference osisRef="Joel.2.23">Joe 2:23</reference>).<div eID="gen16959" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16960" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">whore's forehead--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Jer.8.12">Jr 8:12</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ezek.3.8">Eze 3:8</reference>). <div eID="gen16960" type="x-p"/>
entries.4f698feadb5efda14710c93c57f98b1cba4d0ef0: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv9629"/><div sID="gen16961" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv9629"/><hi type="bold">4. from this time--</hi>not referring, as Michaelis thinks, to the reformation begun the year before, that is, the twelfth of Josiah; it means--now at once, now at last.<div eID="gen16961" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16962" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">me--</hi>contrasted with the "stock" whom they had heretofore called on as "father" (<reference osisRef="Jer.2.27">Jr 2:27</reference>; <reference osisRef="Luke.15.18">Lu 15:18</reference>).<div eID="gen16962" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16963" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">thou art--</hi>rather, "thou wast."<div eID="gen16963" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16964" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">guide of ... youth--</hi>that is, husband (<reference osisRef="Jer.2.2">Jr 2:2</reference>; <reference osisRef="Prov.2.17">Pr 2:17</reference>; <reference osisRef="Hos.2.7">Ho 2:7</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Cor.2.15">15</reference>). Husband and father are the two most endearing of ties. <div eID="gen16964" type="x-p"/>
entries.a73780e6154aa2da842a37177c047e7f216b2d0c: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv9630"/><div sID="gen16965" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv9630"/><hi type="bold">5. he--</hi>"thou," the second person, had preceded. The change to the third person implies a putting away of God to a greater distance from them; instead of repenting and forsaking their idols, they merely deprecate the continuance of their punishment. <reference osisRef="Jer.3.12">Jr 3:12</reference> and <reference osisRef="Ps.103.9">Psa 103:9</reference>, answer their question in the event of their penitence.<div eID="gen16965" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16966" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">spoken and--</hi>rather (God's reply to them), "Thou hast spoken (thus), and yet (all the while) thou hast done evil," &c.<div eID="gen16966" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16967" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">as thou couldest--</hi>with all thy might; with incorrigible persistency [Calvin]. <div eID="gen16967" type="x-p"/>
entries.8089602d5d991a34143261db911d11cf194aab4e: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv9631"/><div sID="gen16968" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv9631"/>6. Jr 3:6-6:30, is a new discourse, delivered in Josiah's reign. It consists of two parts, the former extending to <reference osisRef="Jer.4.3">Jr 4:3</reference>, in which he warns Judah from the example of Israel's doom, and yet promises Israel final restoration; the latter a threat of Babylonian invasion; as Nabopolassar founded the Babylonian empire, 625 B.C., the seventeenth of Josiah, this prophecy is perhaps not earlier than that date (<reference osisRef="Jer.4.5">Jr 4:5</reference>, &c.; <reference osisRef="Jer.5.14">Jr 5:14</reference>, &c.; <reference osisRef="Jer.6.1">Jr 6:1</reference>, &c.; <reference osisRef="Jer.22.1-Jer.22.30">Jr 22:1-30</reference>); and probably not later than the second thorough reformation in the eighteenth year of the same reign.<div eID="gen16968" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16969" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">backsliding--</hi>literally, "apostasy"; not merely apostate, but apostasy itself, the essence of it (<reference osisRef="Jer.3.14">Jr 3:14</reference>, <reference osisRef="Jer.3.22">22</reference>). <div eID="gen16969" type="x-p"/>
entries.25682d80d7f1d322a3f17d2df9dee59c09acfd6a: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv9632"/><div sID="gen16970" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv9632"/><hi type="bold">7. I said--</hi>(<reference osisRef="2Kgs.17.13">2Ki 17:13</reference>).<div eID="gen16970" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16971" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">sister--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Ezek.16.46">Eze 16:46</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ezek.23.2">23:2</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ezek.23.4">4</reference>). <div eID="gen16971" type="x-p"/>
entries.7e33f4ad6c793c98f2926ba18dcc71123c5b723f: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv9633"/><div sID="gen16972" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv9633"/>8. I saw that, though (whereas) it was for this very reason (namely), because backsliding (apostate) Israel had committed adultery I had put her away (<reference osisRef="2Kgs.17.6">2Ki 17:6</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Kgs.17.18">18</reference>), and given her a bill of divorce, yet Judah, &c. (<reference osisRef="Ezek.23.11">Eze 23:11</reference>, &c.).<div eID="gen16972" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16973" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">bill of divorce--</hi>literally, "a writing of cuttings off." The plural implies the completeness of the severance. The use of this metaphor here, as in the former discourse (<reference osisRef="Jer.3.1">Jr 3:1</reference>), implies a close connection between the discourses. The epithets are characteristic; Israel "apostate" (as the Hebrew for "backsliding" is better rendered); Judah, not as yet utterly apostate, but treacherous or faithless.<div eID="gen16973" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16974" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">also--</hi>herself also, like Israel. <div eID="gen16974" type="x-p"/>
entries.b1b40fba6fc889b54b48c0937ff490c5da3b83f3: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv9634"/><div sID="gen16975" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv9634"/><hi type="bold">9. it--</hi>Some take this verse of Judah, to whom the end of <reference osisRef="Jer.3.8">Jr 3:8</reference> refers. But <reference osisRef="Jer.3.10">Jr 3:10</reference> puts Judah in contrast to Israel in this verse. "Yet for all this," referring to the sad example of Israel; if <reference osisRef="Jer.3.9">Jr 3:9</reference> referred to Judah, "she" would have been written in <reference osisRef="Jer.3.10">Jr 3:10</reference>, not "Judah." Translate, "It (the putting away of Israel) had come to pass through ... whoredom; and (that is, for) she (Israel) had defiled the land" &c. [Maurer]. English Version, however, may be explained to refer to Israel.<div eID="gen16975" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16976" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">lightness--</hi>"infamy." [Ewald]. Maurer not so well takes it from the Hebrew root, "voice," "fame." <div eID="gen16976" type="x-p"/>
entries.66f86f7553a6ad6d7914f9bf6666180f140863f4: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv9635"/><div sID="gen16977" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv9635"/><hi type="bold">10. yet--</hi>notwithstanding the lesson given in Israel's case of the fatal results of apostasy.<div eID="gen16977" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16978" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">not ... whole heart--</hi>The reformation in the eighteenth year of Josiah was not thorough on the part of the people, for at his death they relapsed into idolatry (<reference osisRef="2Chr.34.33">2Ch 34:33</reference>; <reference osisRef="Hos.7.14">Ho 7:14</reference>). <div eID="gen16978" type="x-p"/>
entries.ae05c6923875184ea6e1681557b6c14426910f4c: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv9636"/><div sID="gen16979" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv9636"/><hi type="bold">11. justified herself--</hi>has been made to appear almost just (that is, comparatively innocent) by the surpassing guilt of Judah, who adds hypocrisy and treachery to her sin; and who had the example of Israel to warn her, but in vain (compare <reference osisRef="Ezek.16.51">Eze 16:51</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ezek.23.11">23:11</reference>).<div eID="gen16979" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16980" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">more than--</hi>in comparison with. <div eID="gen16980" type="x-p"/>
entries.5fe0e5700b4a8197c4c88d0960887eb4354766e7: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv9637"/><div sID="gen16981" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv9637"/><hi type="bold">12. Go--</hi>not actually; but turn and proclaim towards the north (Media and Assyria, where the ten tribes were located by Tiglath-pileser and Shalmaneser, <reference osisRef="2Kgs.15.29">2Ki 15:29</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Kgs.17.6">17:6</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Kgs.18.9">18:9</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Kgs.18.11">11</reference>).<div eID="gen16981" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16982" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Return ... backsliding--</hi>Hebrew, Shubah, Meshubah, a play on sounds. In order to excite Judah to godly jealousy (<reference osisRef="Rom.11.14">Ro 11:14</reference>), Jehovah addresses the exiled ten tribes of Israel with a loving invitation.<div eID="gen16982" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16983" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">cause ... anger to fall--</hi>literally, "I will not let fall My countenance" (compare <reference osisRef="Gen.4.5">Ge 4:5</reference>, <reference osisRef="Gen.4.6">6</reference>; <reference osisRef="Job.29.3">Job 29:3</reference>), that is, I will not continue to frown on you.<div eID="gen16983" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16984" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">keep--</hi>"anger" is to be supplied (see on <reference osisRef="Jer.3.5">Jr 3:5</reference>). <div eID="gen16984" type="x-p"/>
entries.c78b4fabc7dc3a665a734d37ade966f92e83b880: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv9638"/><div sID="gen16985" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv9638"/><hi type="bold">13. Only acknowledge--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Deut.30.1">De 30:1</reference>, <reference osisRef="Deut.30.3">3</reference>; <reference osisRef="Prov.28.13">Pr 28:13</reference>).<div eID="gen16985" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16986" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">scattered thy ways, &c.--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Jer.2.25">Jr 2:25</reference>). Not merely the calves at Beth-el, but the idols in every direction, were the objects of their worship (<reference osisRef="Ezek.16.15">Eze 16:15</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ezek.24.25">24, 25</reference>). <div eID="gen16986" type="x-p"/>
entries.765770aec138b42e3dfef030c1fc11d26cc88e0a: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv9639"/><div sID="gen16987" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv9639"/><hi type="bold">14. I am married--</hi>literally, "I am Lord," that is, husband to you (so <reference osisRef="Jer.31.32">Jr 31:32</reference>; compare <reference osisRef="Hos.2.19">Ho 2:19</reference>, 20; <reference osisRef="Isa.54.5">Is 54:5</reference>). Gesenius, following the Septuagint version of <reference osisRef="Jer.31.32">Jr 31:32</reference>, and Paul's quotation of it (<reference osisRef="Heb.8.9">He 8:9</reference>), translates, "I have rejected you"; so the corresponding Arabic, and the idea of lordship, may pass into that of looking down upon, and so rejecting. But the Septuagint in this passage translates, "I will be Lord over you." And the "for" has much more force in English Version than in that of Gesenius. The Hebrew hardly admits the rendering though [Hengstenberg].<div eID="gen16987" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16988" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">take you one of a city--</hi>Though but one or two Israelites were in a (foreign) city, they shall not be forgotten; all shall be restored (<reference osisRef="Amos.9.9">Am 9:9</reference>). So, in the spiritual Israel, God gathers one convert here, another there, into His Church; not the least one is lost (<reference osisRef="Matt.18.14">Mt 18:14</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rom.11.5">Ro 11:5</reference>; compare <reference osisRef="Jer.24.5-Jer.24.7">Jr 24:5-7</reference>).<div eID="gen16988" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16989" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">family--</hi>a clan or tribe. <div eID="gen16989" type="x-p"/>
entries.a8fce99181299caebf9d9046696a914423328fcf: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv9640"/><div sID="gen16990" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv9640"/><hi type="bold">15. pastors--</hi>not religious, but civil rulers, as Zerubbabel, Nehemiah (<reference osisRef="Jer.23.4">Jr 23:4</reference>; 2:8). <div eID="gen16990" type="x-p"/>
entries.69e3094be06fb92cd5f8d5cca7cf02546922c3f2: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv9641"/><div sID="gen16991" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv9641"/><hi type="bold">16. they shall say no more--</hi>The Jews shall no longer glory in the possession of the ark; it shall not be missed, so great shall be the blessings of the new dispensation. The throne of the Lord, present Himself, shall eclipse and put out of mind the ark of the covenant and the mercy seat between the cherubim, God's former throne. The ark, containing the two tables of the law, disappeared at the Babylonian captivity, and was not restored to the second temple, implying that the symbolical "glory" was to be superseded by a "greater glory" (<reference osisRef="Hag.2.9">Hag 2:9</reference>).<div eID="gen16991" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16992" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">neither ... visit it--</hi>rather, "neither shall it be missed" (so in <reference osisRef="Jer.23.4">Jr 23:4</reference>).<div eID="gen16992" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16993" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">done--</hi>rather, "neither shall it (the ark) be made (that is, be restored) any more" [Maurer]. <div eID="gen16993" type="x-p"/>
entries.ac375010bd9e59d5822379190ea6f75aa7e2d4d6: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv9642"/><div sID="gen16994" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv9642"/><hi type="bold">17. Jerusalem--</hi>the whole city, not merely the temple. As it has been the center of the Hebrew theocracy, so it shall be the point of attraction to the whole earth (<reference osisRef="Isa.2.2-Isa.2.4">Is 2:2-4</reference>; <reference osisRef="Zech.2.10">Zec 2:10</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Cor.2.11">11</reference>; 14:16-21).<div eID="gen16994" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16995" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">throne of ... Lord--</hi>The Shekinah, the symbol of God's peculiar nearness to Israel (<reference osisRef="Deut.4.7">De 4:7</reference>) shall be surpassed by the antitype, God's own throne in Jerusalem (<reference osisRef="Ps.2.6">Psa 2:6</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Cor.2.8">8</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ezek.34.23">Eze 34:23</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ezek.34.24">24</reference>; <reference osisRef="Zech.2.5">Zec 2:5</reference>).<div eID="gen16995" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16996" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">imagination--</hi>rather, as Margin, "the obstinacy" or stubbornness. <div eID="gen16996" type="x-p"/>
entries.679c5b9c870d3955bb9cd15f107b00259c70b005: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv9643"/><div sID="gen16997" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv9643"/><hi type="bold">18. Judah ... Israel ... together--</hi>Two distinct apostasies, that of Israel and that of Judah, were foretold (<reference osisRef="Jer.3.8">Jr 3:8</reference>, <reference osisRef="Jer.3.10">10</reference>). The two have never been united since the Babylonish captivity; therefore their joint restoration must be still future (<reference osisRef="Isa.11.12">Is 11:12</reference>, <reference osisRef="Isa.11.13">13</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ezek.37.16-Ezek.37.22">Eze 37:16-22</reference>; <reference osisRef="Hos.1.11">Ho 1:11</reference>).<div eID="gen16997" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16998" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">north--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Jer.3.12">Jr 3:12</reference>).<div eID="gen16998" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16999" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">land ... given ... inheritance--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Amos.9.15">Am 9:15</reference>). <div eID="gen16999" type="x-p"/>
entries.54013287a6ee6e75a594846e54c93c3fd8ee1a4d: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv9644"/><div sID="gen17000" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv9644"/>19. The good land covenanted to Abraham is to be restored to his seed.
